body:
What is an electromagnet?

An electromagnet is a magnet whose magnetic field is produced by an electric current. A simple electromagnet can consist of a coil of insulated wire wound around a soft-iron core.

When current flows through the coil, the magnetic field of the coil magnetises the iron core. When the current is switched off, the magnetic field of the coil disappears and the soft-iron core generally loses most of its induced magnetism.

Electromagnets are useful because their magnetic action can be controlled electrically. A magnetic crane, for example, can attract iron or steel objects while current flows and release them when the electromagnet is switched off.

Electromagnet and permanent magnet compared

FeatureElectromagnetPermanent magnet
Source of magnetismElectric current in a coilRetained magnetisation of material
Switching magnetic effectCan be controlled by currentDoes not require current to remain magnetic
Reversing polesReverse current directionRemagnetise in the opposite direction
Typical exampleElectric bell or lifting craneCompass needle or bar magnet

The iron core strengthens a coil's magnetic effect. Its usefulness comes not only from magnetic strength but also from the ability to change the field when the current changes.

Principle of the electric bell

A traditional electric bell uses the magnetic effect of current to produce repeated motion. Its main parts include an electromagnet, a movable iron strip called an armature, a contact screw, a hammer and a gong.

The working sequence is as follows:

  1. When the bell switch closes the circuit, current flows through the coil and makes it an electromagnet.
  2. The electromagnet attracts the nearby iron armature.
  3. The attached hammer strikes the gong, producing sound.
  4. Movement of the armature breaks the electrical contact, so current through the coil stops.
  5. The electromagnet loses its attracting force, and the armature returns to its original position.
  6. The electrical contact is restored and the process repeats rapidly while the bell switch remains pressed.

Why the bell continues ringing

The essential feature of the electric bell is that the electromagnet's action also interrupts its own circuit. This interruption releases the armature, which restores the contact and allows the next cycle to begin.

The repeated sequence of attraction, contact breaking, release and contact restoration produces the ringing sound.

Other simple applications

Electromagnets are used in electrically operated bells, magnetic lifting equipment and devices that need a magnetic force controlled by current. A current-carrying coil may therefore be used either to create a magnetic field or, when combined with movable parts, to produce motion.

Prelims focus

  • An electromagnet produces magnetism through electric current in a coil.
  • A soft-iron core strengthens the magnetic field of an electromagnet.
  • Reversing current in an electromagnet reverses its magnetic poles.
  • An electric bell uses an electromagnet to attract an iron armature.
  • The bell rings repeatedly because its circuit is alternately completed and broken.
  • Trap: A permanent magnet does not need a continuous electric current to maintain its magnetism.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 14, “Electric Current and its Effects,” printed pp. 167–170, sections 14.3–14.5; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 12, “Magnetic Effects of Electric Current,” printed pp. 200–201, section 12.2.4.]

pictures.alt: A labelled electric bell and a four-step cycle show how armature motion breaks and restores the contact, switching coil current off and on.
pictures.caption: An electric bell repeatedly makes and breaks its circuit to operate the hammer.

title: Electromagnets and the Working of an Electric Bell

body:
Force on a current-carrying conductor

An electric current produces a magnetic field. Conversely, when a current-carrying conductor is placed in an external magnetic field, the conductor may experience a magnetic force.

The direction of this force depends on 2 directions: the direction of conventional current and the direction of the magnetic field. When the current and the field are perpendicular, the magnetic force on a straight conductor is greatest under otherwise identical conditions.

Reversing the current reverses the direction of force when the magnetic field remains unchanged. Reversing the magnetic field also reverses the force when the current remains unchanged.

The force provides the basic working principle of an electric motor.

Fleming's left-hand rule

Fleming's left-hand rule determines the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.

Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that all 3 are mutually perpendicular:

  • Forefinger: direction of magnetic field, from north pole towards south pole outside the magnet.
  • Middle finger: direction of conventional current.
  • Thumb: direction of force or resulting motion of the conductor.

This rule applies to the motor effect: an externally supplied current interacts with a magnetic field and produces a force.

Left hand for motor force. The forefinger gives the field, the middle finger gives the current and the thumb gives the force or motion.

Working principle of an electric motor

An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Electric fans, mixers, washing machines and water pumps use motors to produce rotational motion.

The simple DC motor

A basic school-level DC motor contains a rectangular coil of insulated conducting wire placed between magnetic poles. The coil is mounted on an axle so that it can rotate.

When current passes through the coil, its opposite sides carry current in opposite directions. These sides experience magnetic forces in opposite directions. The forces together turn the coil and the axle.

A split-ring commutator is connected to the rotating coil. Stationary brushes make electrical contact with the rotating split ring.

After every half rotation, the split ring reverses the direction of current through the coil. This reversal also reverses the forces on the corresponding coil sides. Since those sides have exchanged positions, the turning effect continues in the same rotational direction.

Why the split ring is important

Without appropriately timed reversal of current, the simple coil would not be driven continuously in one rotational direction by this arrangement. The split-ring commutator allows the coil to keep rotating in the same general direction.

The current reversal happens inside the rotating motor circuit; it is not the same as changing the polarity of the external DC battery after every half turn.

Practical significance

In electric pumps used for household water supply and irrigation, a motor drives a rotating mechanical component that moves water. The electrical energy supplied to the motor is converted into mechanical motion, although some energy is inevitably lost as heat and sound.

This is different from an electric heater, whose intended useful output is heat. Both may draw electrical power, but they use it for different purposes.

Prelims focus

  • A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field can experience a force.
  • The force is greatest when current and magnetic field are perpendicular, other conditions remaining the same.
  • Fleming's left-hand rule determines the direction of the force.
  • An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
  • In a simple DC motor, the split-ring commutator reverses coil current after every half rotation.
  • Trap: The right-hand thumb rule gives the field around a current; Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current in an external field.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 12, “Magnetic Effects of Electric Current,” printed pp. 202–203, section 12.3; NCERT, Science, Class 10, older unabridged version of the same chapter, section 12.4, “Electric Motor,” consulted through the Philoid NCERT chapter text on 2 November 2026.]

title: Magnetic Force, Fleming's Left-Hand Rule and Electric Motors

body:
Can a magnetic field produce an electric current?

A current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field. The reverse connection is equally important: a changing magnetic field associated with a conducting circuit can induce a potential difference.

The English scientist Michael Faraday demonstrated electromagnetic induction in 1831. His work established the principle on which electric generators operate.

Electromagnetic induction is the production of an induced electromotive force (emf) when the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes. Magnetic flux measures the magnetic field passing through the circuit's enclosed area and depends on the field, area and orientation. If the induced circuit is closed, an induced current can flow.

Moving a magnet near a coil

Consider a coil connected to a sensitive current-detecting instrument called a galvanometer. A bar magnet is brought near the coil.

  • Magnet moving towards the coil: The magnetic field associated with the coil changes. An induced potential difference appears, and current flows if the circuit is complete.
  • Magnet held stationary near the coil: If the magnetic field associated with the coil remains unchanged, no continuing current is induced by this arrangement.
  • Magnet moving away from the coil: The change occurs in the opposite sense, and the induced current reverses direction.

Moving the coil while keeping the magnet stationary can also produce induction. The important condition is a change in the magnetic flux linked with the coil, not motion of a particular object by itself.

Moving a magnet more rapidly can produce a greater induced potential difference because the magnetic field associated with the coil changes more rapidly.

A stationary magnet can produce a magnetic field without producing a continuous induced current in a nearby stationary coil. For induction in the coil, the magnetic flux linked with it must change. A closed circuit is required for induced current, although an induced potential difference can exist without a complete external current path.

Fleming's right-hand rule

For a straight conductor moving through a magnetic field, Fleming's right-hand rule helps determine the direction of induced conventional current.

Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand so that they are mutually perpendicular:

  • Forefinger: direction of magnetic field.
  • Thumb: direction of motion of the conductor.
  • Middle finger: direction of induced conventional current.

Unlike the left-hand rule used for the force in a motor, the right-hand rule is used to find the direction of current generated by suitable motion in a magnetic field.

Electric generator

An electric generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. It works on the principle of electromagnetic induction.

In a simple generator, a conducting coil rotates in a magnetic field. As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux linked with it changes, producing an induced potential difference. If the external circuit is closed, current flows.

The generator does not create energy from nothing. Mechanical work supplied to rotate the coil is converted into electrical energy, with some inevitable energy losses.

Alternating current and direct current

Direct current (DC) flows in one direction in the external circuit. Cells and batteries are familiar sources of DC.

Alternating current (AC) periodically reverses its direction. In a simple rotating-coil AC generator, the induced current reverses direction after every half rotation.

A basic AC generator uses separate slip rings connected to the rotating coil. A simple DC generator can use a split-ring commutator to give a unidirectional output in the external circuit.

Keeping the 3 direction rules separate

RuleKnown directionDirection obtained
Right-hand thumb ruleCurrent in a straight wireMagnetic field around the wire
Fleming's left-hand ruleCurrent and external magnetic fieldForce or motion
Fleming's right-hand ruleConductor motion and magnetic fieldInduced current

Prelims focus

  • Faraday demonstrated electromagnetic induction in 1831.
  • A changing magnetic field associated with a coil can induce a potential difference.
  • Reversing the motion of a magnet relative to a coil reverses the induced current in the simple arrangement described.
  • Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of induced current.
  • A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  • Trap: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy; a generator performs the reverse conversion.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, older unabridged version of “Magnetic Effects of Electric Current,” sections 12.5–12.6, “Electromagnetic Induction” and “Electric Generator,” consulted through the Philoid NCERT chapter text on 2 November 2026.]
